messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo source: Sinusoidal current $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, $C_p \approx 25\text{ nF}$.
    *   $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 0.76\text{ V}$.
    *   Target output: $V_{out} \in [1.8\text{ V}, 3.6\text{ V}]$.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$
        *   $dV \le 0.02\text{ V}$
    *   Crucial observation: $V_{oc} \approx 0.76\text{ V}$ is much lower than the required $1.8\text{ V}$. A simple bridge rectifier (FBR) will not work because the piezo voltage cannot overcome the diode drops and reach 1.8V unless the load is extremely light or the source very strong (as seen in the FBR reference results).
    *   To boost the voltage, I need a DC-DC converter. Since it's a piezoelectric source, a Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) or a similar switching topology is ideal. SSHI essentially flips the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks, increasing the available voltage.

    *   *Topology 1: SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor)*.
        *   SSHI uses a switch and an inductor to invert the charge on $C_p$ every half-cycle.
        *   The current then flows through a rectifier into the storage capacitor.
        *   The inversion increases the voltage swing of $C_p$.
        *   Circuit: Piezo terminals (pzp, pzn). An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ across the piezo (or one terminal to ground). A rectifier (full bridge or half bridge) from the piezo to the output.
        *   Wait, a simpler version: SSHI usually puts the inductor in parallel with the piezo and switches it. Then it rectifies the resulting voltage.
        *   Let's try a modified SSHI:
            *   S1: Switch and Inductor across the piezo to flip voltage.
            *   Rectifier: Full bridge from piezo to $C_{out}$.
            *   Since $V_{oc}$ is very low, we might need a boost converter or a very efficient SSHI.
            *   Actually, a common SSHI topology: $C_p$ is in parallel with a switch and inductor. When the switch closes, the energy in $C_p$ transfers to $L$, then back to $C_p$ with opposite polarity. The rectifier (full bridge) harvests the peaks.

    *   *Topology 2: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction)*.
        *   SECE separates the harvesting from the source.
        *   A switch connects the piezo to an inductor, then the inductor is connected to the storage cap.
        *   This can be more efficient for very low $V_{oc}$.

    *   *Topology 3: Simple Boost (if possible)*.
        *   Hard to do without a controller. The provided `SYNC` controller is specifically designed for piezo extrema.

    *   Let's refine the SSHI structure:
        *   Piezo (pzp, pzn).
        *   Inductor $L1$ and Switch $S1$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   Rectifier (4 diodes) from pzp/pzn to $V_{out}$.
        *   Wait, if the switch and inductor are in parallel with the piezo, the bridge rectifier is also in parallel. This is the standard SSHI.
        *   Wait, the `SYNC` controller's `ton` is very short (up to 1ms). $\pi \sqrt{LC_p}$ for $L=10\text{mH}$ and $C_p=25\text{nF}$ is $\approx 15\text{ $\mu$s}$. This fits.

    *   Wait, $V_{oc} \approx 0.76\text{V}$. Even with SSHI, the peak voltage might only be a few times $V_{oc}$. If $V_{oc}=0.76\text{V}$, SSHI can potentially push the voltage higher. But if we need $1.8\text{V}$ at the output, and we have diode drops (DSCH $\approx 0.25\text{V} \times 2 = 0.5\text{V}$), the piezo voltage needs to reach $1.8 + 0.5 = 2.3\text{V}$.
    *   The voltage flip in SSHI: $V_{flip} \approx V_{peak} \cdot (1 + \text{efficiency})$. The voltage builds up over cycles.
    *   Let's try the SSHI topology:
        *   S1: switch, L1: inductor. Parallel to piezo.
        *   Full bridge rectifier: D1, D2, D3, D4.
        *   Storage: C_out.
        *   Zener: DZ33 to clamp at 3.3V.

    *   *Alternative: Parallel-SSHI (P-SSHI)*.
        *   The switch and inductor are in parallel with the piezo.
        *   The rectifier is also in parallel.
        *   The switch closes at the peaks to invert the voltage.

    *   *Let's reconsider the "boost" need*.
        The reference FBR failed mostly on $V_{avg}$ (too low). SSHI improves the voltage extracted from $C_p$ by avoiding the "charge-waste" that occurs when the piezo voltage is lower than the output voltage.

    *   Proposed Design 1 (SSHI):
        *   L1: pzp to n1
        *   S1: n1 to pzn (ctrl: G1)
        *   D1: pzp to out
        *   D2: pzn to out
        *   D3: 0 to pzp
        *   D4: 0 to pzn
        *   C1: out to 0
        *   DZ1: 0 to out (model DZ33)
        *   G1: SYNC (edges: both, phase: 0, ton: $\approx 15\text{ $\mu$s}$)

    *   *Wait*, is there a more efficient way? Maybe a "Charge Pump" style? But we only have `SYNC` and basic components.
    *   Let's try a "Half-Bridge" SSHI if a full bridge is too lossy? No, full bridge is standard.

    *   Let's check the $V_{oc}$ again. $I_p = 12\text{ $\mu$A}, f=100\text{ Hz}, C_p=25\text{ nF} \implies V_{peak} = 12\text{e-6} / (2 \pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}) = 12 / (2 \pi \cdot 2.5\text{e-3}) = 12 / 0.0157 = 764\text{ V}$?
    *   Wait, calculation: $12 \times 10^{-6} / (2 \cdot 3.1415 \cdot 100 \cdot 25 \times 10^{-9}) = 12 \times 10^{-6} / (1.57 \times 10^{-5}) = 0.764\text{ V}$.
    *   Yes, $0.76\text{ V}$. My previous thought was correct. This is very low.
    *   Can SSHI reach $1.8\text{ V} + 0.5\text{ V} = 2.3\text{ V}$?
        In SSHI, the voltage across $C_p$ can reach a steady state $V_{max} = \frac{4 I_p}{2\pi f C_p \cdot \text{losses}}$. Roughly, it increases the effective source voltage. However, the "gain" is limited.

    *   Is there another topology?
        Maybe the "Inductive Boost" using the `SYNC` switch?
        If we put the inductor in series and switch it?
        Let's try:
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to 0 (ctrl: G1)
        D1: n1 to out
        This is a boost converter.
        When S1 is closed, L1 charges from pzp.
        When S1 opens, L1 discharges into `out` via D1.
        The `SYNC` controller can do this at the peaks.
        Wait, the piezo is a current source.
        If S1 is closed, the current $I_p$ flows through L1 and S1.
        This might be more effective for boosting.

    *   Let's try two different SSHI-like approaches:
        1.  **Standard SSHI**: Inductor/switch in parallel with piezo, full-bridge rectifier to output.
        2.  **Boost-like SSHI**: Inductor in series with the piezo, switched to ground, then rectified.

    *   Let's refine the Standard SSHI:
        *   Components:
            *   L1 (pzp, n1), S1 (n1, pzn) -> Inverter.
            *   D1 (pzp, out), D2 (pzn, out), D3 (0, pzp), D4 (0, pzn) -> Bridge.
            *   C1 (out, 0) -> Storage.
            *   G1 (SYNC): ton $\approx 15\text{ $\mu$s}$, edges: both.

    *   Let's refine the Boost-like approach (called "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" - SECE - loosely):
        *   L1 (pzp, n1)
        *   S1 (n1, 0) -> Switch to ground.
        *   D1 (n1, out) -> Boost diode.
        *   C1 (out, 0) -> Storage.
        *   G1 (SYNC): edges: pos (or both), ton: very short.
        *   Wait, for a boost to work, the inductor must store energy. When S1 is closed, $L$ is in parallel with the piezo (sort of). When S1 opens, the inductor voltage spikes and pushes current through D1 to `out`.

    *   Let's consider the power constraints. $S_4$ is the weakest: $I_p = 8\text{ $\mu$A}, R_L = 22\text{ M}\Omega$.
        Power needed $\approx (1.8)^2 / 22\text{e6} = 1.47 \times 10^{-7}\text{ W} = 0.147\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        The `SYNC` controller costs $0.5\text{ $\mu$A} \times 1.8\text{ V} = 0.9\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        Wait! The `SYNC` cost (0.9 $\mu$W) is much higher than the load power (0.147 $\mu$W).
        This means the energy harvester must produce at least $0.9 + 0.147 = 1.047\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        Is that possible?
        $P_{piezo} \approx \frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2 f = 0.5 \cdot 25\text{e-9} \cdot (0.76)^2 \cdot 100 = 7.2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ W} = 0.72\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        Uh oh. $0.72\text{ $\mu$W}$ is the *total* available energy from the piezo if we extract everything.
        If the `SYNC` controller costs $0.9\text{ $\mu$W}$, it's impossible to power the load and the controller using the piezo alone... unless $V_{out}$ is lower, but it must be $1.8\text{V}$.
        Let me re-read: "for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost)".
        $0.5\text{ $\mu$A} \cdot 1.8\text{ V} = 0.9\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        And $S_4$ load: $1.8\text{ V} / 22\text{ M}\Omega = 81\text{ nA}$.
        Total current needed: $500\text{ nA} + 81\text{ nA} = 581\text{ nA}$.
        Total energy per cycle: $P/f = 1.047\text{ $\mu$W} / 100\text{ Hz} = 10.47\text{ nJ}$.
        Available energy per cycle: $\frac{1}{2} C_p V_{oc}^2 = 0.5 \cdot 25\text{e-9} \cdot (0.76)^2 = 7.2\text{ nJ}$.
        It seems the budget is very tight. I must use as few `SYNC` controllers as possible (only one).

    *   Wait, the reference FBR used *no* `SYNC` and failed because $V_{avg}$ was too low. FBR has no power cost.
        Can I use a passive boost? No.
        Is there a way to reach 1.8V without `SYNC`?
        The only way to increase voltage without `SYNC` is a transformer or a charge pump (which needs a clock).
        But the `SYNC` controller is the only way to get "active" switching.
        Let's re-calculate $P_{piezo}$ for $S_3$ (strongest):
        $I_p = 40\text{ $\mu$A}, V_{oc} = 40\text{e-6} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}) = 2.54\text{ V}$.
        $P = 0.5 \cdot 25\text{e-9} \cdot (2.54)^2 \cdot 100 = 8.1\text{ $\mu$W}$. This one easily passes.
        $S_4$ (weakest): $I_p = 8\text{ $\mu$A}, V_{oc} = 0.51\text{ V}$.
        $P = 0.5 \cdot 25\text{e-9} \cdot (0.51)^2 \cdot 100 = 0.32\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        If the `SYNC` cost is $0.9\text{ $\mu$W}$, $S_4$ can *never* be powered by a `SYNC` circuit.
        Wait, is the $0.5\text{ $\mu$A}$ only when the switch is active? No, "supply current drawn from out".
        Is there a way to meet $S_4$ without `SYNC`?
        If $V_{oc} = 0.51\text{ V}$ and $V_{out} = 1.8\text{ V}$, a passive rectifier will *never* work.
        Is there a mistake in my $V_{oc}$ calculation?
        $V = I / (2\pi f C)$.
        $S_4: 8\text{e-6} / (2 \cdot \pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}) = 8\text{e-6} / 1.57\text{e-5} = 0.51\text{ V}$.
        This is correct.
        Wait, the FBR reference results for $S_4$: $V_{avg} = 0.334\text{ V}$.
        This confirms $V_{oc}$ is low.
        If the `SYNC` controller cost is $0.9\text{ $\mu$W}$ and the total available power is $0.32\text{ $\mu$W}$, then `SYNC` is impossible for $S_4$.
        Wait... let me re-read the "SCREENED" section.
        "If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them, the design is reported back... and is not tuned or simulated further."
        This screening *excludes* the `SYNC` cost! It only checks the power delivered to $R_L$.
        So the `SYNC` cost is only counted during the full simulation, not the screening.
        But in the full simulation, the $0.5\text{ $\mu$A}$ *will* be drawn.
        If $P_{piezo} < P_{sync}$, the capacitor $C_{out}$ will drain, and $V_{out}$ will drop.
        This means the only way to pass $S_4$ is if $P_{piezo} > P_{sync} + P_{load}$.
        But $0.32\text{ $\mu$W} < 0.9\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        Is there any way to avoid the `SYNC` cost?
        The only way is to not use `SYNC`. But without `SYNC`, you can't boost.
        Wait, let me re-calculate $P_{piezo}$ more carefully.
        Is $I_p$ the *average* current or *peak* current?
        "sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t)". $I_p$ is the peak.
        The power available from a current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ into a capacitor $C_p$ is $P = \frac{1}{2} I_p^2 / (\omega C_p)$? No, that's not right.
        The voltage is $V(t) = \frac{I_p}{\omega C_p} \sin(\omega t + \phi)$.
        The average power is $P = \frac{1}{T} \int V I dt = \frac{1}{T} \int \frac{I_p^2}{\omega C_p} \sin^2(\omega t) dt = \frac{I_p^2}{2 \omega C_p}$.
        Let's re-calculate for $S_4$:
        $P = (8\text{e-6})^2 / (2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{e-9}) = 64\text{e-12} / (3.14\text{e-5}) = 2.03\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        Aha! $2.03\text{ $\mu$W}$ is much better! It's more than the $0.9\text{ $\mu$W}$ cost.
        My previous power formula $\frac{1}{2} C V^2 f$ was for a *voltage* source. For a *current* source, it's $\frac{I_p^2}{2 \omega C_p}$.
        Let's check $S_1$:
        $P = (12\text{e-6})^2 / (3.14\text{e-5}) = 1.44\text{e-11} / 3.14\text{e-5} = 4.58\text{ $\mu$W}$.
        Ok, so `SYNC` is viable.

    *   Now, back to topology. I'll propose two:
        1.  **Standard SSHI**: The most robust way to increase voltage from a piezo.
        2.  **Modified Boost SSHI**: To see if it's more efficient.

    *   Standard SSHI details:
        *   $C_p$ is the piezo capacitance.
        *   $L$ and $S$ are in parallel with $C_p$.
        *   The rectifier is also in parallel with $C_p$.
        *   When $S$ closes, the energy in $C_p$ is transferred to $L$, then back to $C_p$ (inverting the voltage).
        *   This happens at the peaks of the voltage (which are the zero-crossings of the current $I_p$).
        *   The `SYNC` controller "closes its switches... at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero crossings of the piezo current." This is exactly what we need.

    *   Circuit for Standard SSHI:
        *   S1: switch, L1: inductor.
        *   S1 and L1 are in series, and this branch is in parallel with the piezo (pzp to pzn).
        *   Full bridge:
            *   D1: pzp to out
            *   D2: pzn to out
            *   D3: 0 to pzp
            *   D4: 0 to pzn
        *   Cout: out to 0.
        *   Zener DZ33: 0 to out.

    *   Wait, let's refine the bridge. If pzp is at a high positive voltage, D1 conducts to `out`. If pzn is at a high positive voltage, D2 conducts to `out`. This is correct.
    *   Wait, the "return" diodes D3 and D4: "full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]".
        This is:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        Wait, that's not a full bridge. A full bridge should be:
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp (Wait, if pzp is negative, D3 conducts from 0 to pzp)
        D4: 0 -> pzn (Wait, if pzn is negative, D4 conducts from 0 to pzn)
        Actually, this *is* a full bridge. Let's trace:
        Current from piezo:
        When $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$: $pzp \to D1 \to out \to load \to 0 \to D4 \to pzn$. (If $V_{pzn}$ is low).
        This is a standard bridge.

    *   Let's double check the SSHI inversion:
        $L$ and $S$ must be in parallel with the piezo.
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to pzn
        This is in parallel with the piezo (pzp to pzn).

    *   Wait, I can also try a "Half-Bridge" SSHI to reduce diode drops.
        If pzn is tied to 0 (ground), the piezo is just between pzp and 0.
        But the piezo is a current source between pzp and pzn. I can't just ground pzn.
        Wait, the piezo model is "between nodes pzp and pzn".
        If I ground pzn:
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to pzn (which is 0)
        D1: pzp to out
        D2: 0 to pzp (Wait, this is not helping)
        Actually, a full bridge is safer.

    *   Is there any other topology?
        Maybe "Parallel-SSHI" where the inductor is not in parallel with the piezo but in a different configuration?
        Actually, let's stick with the standard SSHI and maybe one more.
        How about a "Buck-Boost" like structure?
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to 0
        D1: n1 to out
        This is the "Boost-like" I mentioned. Let's try it as the second proposal.
        For the Boost-like:
        When S1 is closed, $L$ stores energy.
